pred_diagnosis: Lemma AddSub has no precondition, yet its ensures clause calls Sub(x, y), and Sub requires !Less(x, y). The ensures clause is therefore not well-formed. The counterexample shows this: with x == Zero and y == Suc(...), Less(x, y) holds and Sub is undefined. The equation Add(Sub(x, y), y) == x also cannot hold when x < y. The precondition requires !Less(x, y), present in the original book version, is missing. Every caller (AddMulSucSubEqAddMul) already establishes !Less(x0, y) before calling AddSub.

The failing assertion is the final assert in lemmaInvSubsetTakeValueFromC, which restates its ensures: multiset(b[..i+j+1]) == multiset(c[..i+1]) + multiset(d[..j]). Unlike the symmetric lemmaInvSubsetTakeValueFromD, which requires b[i+j] == d[j], this lemma never states that the newly written element b[i+j] equals c[i]. Without that link, adding b[i+j] to the prefix of b says nothing about adding c[i] to the prefix of c. The counterexample (i = 2283 < |c|) has b[i+j] differing from c[i], so the multiset equality cannot follow from the preconditions. At the call site in MergeLoop, b[i+j] := c[i] has just been executed, so the missing precondition holds there and can safely be added.

The precondition `a.Length > -1` is always true, so it permits an empty array, contradicting the intended non-empty requirement. With a.Length == 0 and i initialized to 1, the outer loop invariant `i <= a.Length` (line 35) is false on loop entry. The invariant `sorted(a, 0, i)` would also be ill-formed. Requiring a non-empty array establishes 1 <= a.Length, so the invariant holds initially.

The constructor's precondition `requires capacity > -1` admits capacity == 0. Valid() demands `this.capacity > 0`, so with capacity = 0 the constructor cannot establish its postcondition `ensures Valid()`. This matches the counterexample, where capacity = 0. The precondition is too weak: it should require a strictly positive capacity, which is also what a fixed-capacity cache that can hold items needs.

The method get has no precondition, so nothing is known about the object's state on entry. Line 80 asserts that a present key has a non-negative value, and the postcondition ensures Valid() requires capacity > 0, |cacheMap| <= capacity, and positive frequencies and non-negative values. None of these can be proved because the cache may be in an arbitrary state when get is called; the counterexample shows capacity = -2437. Every other method that ensures Valid() (getLFUKey, put) also takes it as a precondition, but get omits it. Adding requires Valid() lets the body prove the assertion. It also lets it re-establish Valid(), since updating an existing key keeps |cacheMap| the same, keeps the value, and increases the frequency.

The precondition `a.Length > -1` is always true, so it does not rule out an empty array. With a.Length = 0, the statement `m := a[0]` at the start of MaxA indexes out of range. That access must be safe before the loop can even be reached, and the invariants `1 <= i <= a.Length` and the exists-clause cannot hold on entry for an empty array. The intended behavior is a non-empty array, so the precondition should require a.Length > 0.

The precondition of queryFast is too weak. It allows j up to a.Length + 1, but sum(a, i, j) in the postcondition and the lemma aux both require j <= a.Length. With j == a.Length + 1, which the counterexample shows (j = c.Length = a.Length + 1), the ensures clause sum(a, i, j) is not well-formed. The call aux(a, c, i, j) also violates aux's precondition. So the method's precondition cannot be bridged to its postcondition. The bound should be a.Length, since the prefix array c has indices 0..a.Length and a range over a ends at a.Length at most.

The precondition `1<=x< (a.Length) + 1` allows x == a.Length, which is not a position inside the array. The counterexample has x = 6136 = a.Length. In that case the second loop starts with i == a.Length and never runs. The method then sets p := a.Length-1, which is less than x, so the postcondition x<=p<a.Length is false on the final return path. The precondition is too weak: it must keep x strictly inside the array so that p = a.Length-1 >= x always holds.

The method has no precondition bounding x. The only requirement is a.Length != 0. The first loop starts with i := 1 and needs invariant 0 <= i <= x, which fails on entry when x == 0. When x > a.Length, the invariants and the body read a[j] and a[i] out of range. The second loop sets i := x and needs x <= i <= a.Length, which fails on entry when x > a.Length. The intended behavior says x is a position inside the array with at least one element before it, which is also needed for 'exists i :: 0 <= i < x && a[i] == m'. So the precondition must state 1 <= x < a.Length.

The row-monotonicity precondition bounds j' by a.Length1 - 1 instead of a.Length1, so the last column is excluded from the ordering. The loop starts at n = a.Length1-1. When a[m,n] < key the body does m := m+1, which is only safe if every a[m,j] with j <= n is also < key, i.e. a[m,j] <= a[m,n]. For n = a.Length1-1 the weakened precondition does not give this. So Dafny cannot show the key still lies in rows m+1.. and columns 0..n (invariant at line 11). It also cannot show m+1 < a.Length0 (invariant at line 10), which depends on that existence fact. This matches the counterexample with m = 0 and n = Length1-1.

mroot3's precondition was weakened to n>=-1, unlike the other two methods. When n = -1 the loop starts with r = 0 and y = 0. The invariant conjunct r*r<=n becomes 0<=-1, which is false, and y>=r+1 becomes 0>=1, which is also false. So the invariant cannot hold on entry. The postcondition also cannot hold for a negative n. The intended behavior is an integer square root of a non-negative number.

mroot2 is missing the precondition n>=0 that mroot1 and mroot3 both have. With no requires clause, n can be negative (the counterexample uses n = -10391). After r:=n, the invariant conjunct 0<=r<=n is false, so the invariant cannot be established on loop entry. The postcondition r>=0 && r*r<=n is also unsatisfiable for negative n. When n>=0, r=n gives 0<=r<=n and n<(n+1)*(n+1), so the invariant holds on entry.

mmaxvalue1 has the precondition 'requires v.Length>-1', which allows an empty array (v.Length = 0). Its body calls mmaximum1(v), and mmaximum1 requires v.Length>0, so the call's precondition cannot be proved. The intended behavior is defined only for non-empty arrays, and 'm in v[..]' is impossible for an empty array anyway. The precondition of mmaxvalue1 is too weak and should match mmaxvalue2.

The precondition of binarySearchRec says 'forall k::0<=k<c ==> v[k]<= (elem) + 1'. This only bounds the elements before c by elem+1, not by elem. In the base case c==f+1 the method returns p:=c-1, and the postcondition 'forall u::0<=u<=p ==> v[u]<=elem' must then follow directly from the precondition about indices below c. With the weakened bound it does not follow: the counterexample has c=1, v[0]=2329, elem=2328, so v[0] <= elem+1 holds but v[0] <= elem fails. The intended precondition, mirroring the iterative loop invariant, bounds those elements by elem itself. That bound is also what the recursive call with c=m+1 establishes after checking v[m]<=elem, using sortedness.

The predicate sorted_seg has no precondition, but its body indexes a[l] and a[k] for every i <= l <= k < j. Dafny checks predicate bodies for well-formedness on their own, so with arbitrary i and j (e.g. i = -39, or j = 7681 > a.Length) these accesses can be out of bounds. That produces the two 'index out of range' errors at line 4. Every call site already passes bounds within 0..a.Length: (c,i), (c,i+1), (c,f), (i,f) and (j,f), all under 0 <= c <= i <= j <= f <= a.Length. So the predicate only needs a requires clause stating that range.

The precondition of predicate sorted_seg was weakened to 'j <= a.Length + 1'. That allows j == a.Length + 1, so with k < j we get k == a.Length. The body then reads a[l] and a[k] out of bounds, and Dafny cannot prove the predicate body well-formed. The counterexamples show exactly this case: a.Length = 0 with j = 1, and a.Length = 39 with j = 40. The upper bound for an excluded endpoint must be a.Length, not a.Length + 1. Every use in selSort (c, i, f all <= a.Length) already satisfies the tighter bound.

The predicate sorted_seg's precondition `0 <= i <= j+1 <= a.Length + 1` is too weak for its own body. It allows j == a.Length, so the quantifier can take l or k equal to a.Length, and then a[l] and a[k] are out of range. The counterexample shows this: a.Length = 1, i = 0, j = 1 means k = 1 is in range of the quantifier but a[1] is invalid. Because the precondition does not establish that every index in [i, j] is a valid array index, the body is not well-formed. The bound must be j+1 <= a.Length. All existing call sites still satisfy it: sorted_seg(a,0,a.Length-1), sorted_seg(a,0,i-1) with i <= a.Length, and sorted_seg(a,j+1,i) with i < a.Length inside the outer loop.

The precondition of segMaxSum is only `v.Length>0` and says nothing about the range of i. When i is negative, the invariant 0<=j<=i fails at entry with j=0. When i >= v.Length, the ensures clause Sum(v,k,i+1) and SumMaxToRight(v,i,s) are ill-formed, as are the invariants and the access v[j+1]. The method needs the same bound on i that segSumaMaxima2 has.

The first precondition of LemmaAscendingSubsequence has an off-by-one error. It says `i <= (|q1|-|q2|) + 1`, which lets `i + |q2|` be `|q1| + 1`. That allows the slice `q1[i..i+|q2|]` to run past the end of q1. For example, with i = 2 and |q1| = 1, the lower bound i exceeds |q1|. With i = 0, |q1| = 1 and |q2| = 2, the upper bound exceeds |q1|. So the requires clause is not well-formed, which causes the 'lower bound out of range' and 'upper bound ... above length' errors. Because the slice equality cannot be relied on, the precondition does not give a valid fact that q2 is a contiguous sub-range of q1. As a result, the lemma's empty body cannot bridge from Ascending(q1) to the postcondition Ascending(q2). Both call sites (offset 0 for qleft, and offset |qleft|+1 for qright) satisfy the tighter bound `i <= |q1| - |q2|`, so removing the `+ 1` fixes the lemma without breaking its callers.

pred_repair: requires forall k:: k in NumbersInSequence(q) ==> k < i
pred_diagnosis: lemma_all_small is missing the precondition that every element of NumbersInSequence(q) is below i. Its mirror lemma_all_big has the matching 'k > i' requires, but lemma_all_small only requires that each q[k] is in NumbersInSequence(q), which holds for any sequence. So nothing relates the elements to i, and the postcondition 'forall j :: 0 <= j < |q| ==> q[j] < i' cannot be proved. The counterexample i = 0, q[22] = 7719 shows this. Because the lemma's contract is too weak, InsertBST's call to it does not deliver the fact needed for Ascending(new_left_nums + [i]) and BST(t). The verifier then struggles to prove those facts unaided, which contributes to the timeout of InsertBST.

PrimeMap is {:autocontracts}, so every method implicitly ensures Valid(): each key maps to true exactly when it is prime. InsertPrime unconditionally sets database[n] := true, but nothing requires n to be prime. With n = 4 the method stores database[4] = true while prime(4) is false. Valid() is then violated at return, so the implicit postcondition cannot be proved. The method is meant to insert an already-known prime, but that assumption is missing from its precondition.

Mult's precondition is weakened to x >= -1, but the intended behavior multiplies two non-negative integers. With x = -1, as in the counterexample, the else branch asserts x-1 >= 0, which is false (-2 >= 0), so the assertion at line 155 fails. The precondition is also too weak to justify the recursive call Mult(x-1, y), which would need x-1 >= -1, and for termination the decreasing measure x must stay non-negative. Requiring x >= 0 makes x-1 >= 0 hold in the else branch, where x != 0 means x >= 1.

The first precondition of LinearSearch3, `requires |s1| <= (data.Length) + 1`, is off by one. It allows |s1| == data.Length + 1. Then for i == |s1|-1, the second precondition reads data[data.Length-1-i] == data[-1], which is index out of range (line 75; the counterexample has data.Length = 0, |s1| = 1). The same weak bound breaks the indexing in the loop body and asserts, e.g. data[data.Length - n1 + n] with n1 = data.Length + 1 and n = 0 gives index -1. It also makes `assert |s1| <= data.Length` fail after the loop. Because the precondition cannot rule out a sequence longer than the array, the facts that the loop body and the post-loop asserts depend on are never established.

LinearSearch3 is missing the precondition |s1| <= data.Length, which LinearSearch1 and LinearSearch2 both have. Without it, the requires clause `forall i :: 0 <= i < |s1| ==> s1[i] == data[data.Length-1-i]` is not well-formed: when |s1| > data.Length (e.g. data.Length = 36, |s1| = 39), the index data.Length-1-i goes negative. The same gap breaks the body. With n1 = |s1| > data.Length, the access data[data.Length - n1 + n] in the loop guard check and in the asserts is out of range (e.g. data.Length = 0, |s1| = 1239, n = 0). The asserts after the loop also index data[data.Length-1] and data[data.Length-n1] out of range. Because the precondition does not bound |s1| by data.Length, none of these array accesses can be proved in bounds, starting from loop entry.

RotateLeft has the precondition 'requires a.Length > -1', which is always true and so allows an empty array. With a.Length == 0, the postcondition 'a[a.Length - 1]' indexes position -1, giving the index-out-of-range error in the ensures clause. At loop entry n == 0 and a.Length - 1 == -1, so the invariant '0 <= n <= a.Length - 1' fails on entry (and 'a[n]' would also be out of range). Rotating needs at least one element, so the precondition must require a non-empty array.

RotateRight has no precondition requiring a non-empty array. When a.Length == 0, the postcondition's a[0] and old(a[a.Length-1]) are out of range, which is the well-formedness error at line 393. At loop entry n == 1, so the invariant 1 <= n <= a.Length fails because 1 > 0, which is the initiation error at line 397. The precondition requires a.Length > 0, present in the original RotateRight and also in RotateLeft, is missing.

UpWhileNotEqual has no precondition. Every other method that counts over N requires 0 <= N, but this one does not. If N is negative (e.g. N = -1), then after i := 0 the invariant 0 <= i <= N is false at loop entry. The missing precondition is what breaks initiation. It is also needed for termination (decreases N - i) and matches the intended non-negative bound.

pred_repair: requires forall p,q | i <= p < q < i+n :: a[p] <= a[q];
pred_diagnosis: Search2PowLoop has no sortedness precondition, unlike Search1000 and Search2PowRecursive. The loop body tests only one element, a[k+c]. If a[k+c] < x, it sets k := k+c+1 and relies on invariant 66 to conclude that every element below the new k is < x. Otherwise it relies on invariant 67 to conclude that every element from k+c up is >= x. Both conclusions need the segment a[i..i+n) to be sorted. Without that, Dafny cannot show the two invariants are maintained. The counterexamples use unsorted arrays: a[5248]=3609 but a[7721]=-1, and a[22425]=867 but a[22428]=866. The invariants hold on entry and the spec is otherwise fine. The missing sortedness precondition is the cause.

The override check fails because the trait declares `at` with the off-by-one precondition `requires 0 <= index < (|s|) + 1`, which allows index == |s|. The class implementation of `at` (line 214) requires `0 <= index < |s|`. That is strictly stronger than the trait's precondition, so Dafny rejects the override: a refining method must accept every input its parent trait accepts. The class precondition cannot be weakened instead, because the body `return s[index]` and the ensures `s[index] == x` would then be out of range for index == |s|. The trait's precondition is the faulty specification and must be tightened to the valid index range.

The class implementation of CircularLinkedList.removeAtIndex omits the precondition 'requires Valid()' that the trait declares. Without it, the method body cannot assume |l| <= capacity on entry. In the counterexample, |l| = 3 and capacity = 1 at entry, and removing one element leaves |l| = 2 > capacity. So the postcondition 'ensures Valid()' cannot be proved.

Sqare2 has the precondition `requires a>=0`, which admits a = 0. The first assertion `assert 1 <= 1 <= a && 1==1*1` (line 126) and the loop invariant `1 <= y <= a` need a >= 1. With a = 0 the invariant cannot be established on loop entry, so the precondition is too weak.

ComputeFact2 has no precondition, so n may be negative (counterexample n = -1). The postcondition f == factorial(n) then calls factorial outside its requires n >= 0 (error at line 48). The invariant 0 <= x <= n also fails on entry, because x = 0 > n = -1 (error at line 53). The missing requires n >= 0, which ComputeFact has, is what should establish the invariant at loop entry and make the ensures well-formed.

Init's precondition `requires c > -1` allows c == 0. With c == 0, capacity becomes 0, so the conjunct `capacity > 0` in Valid() is false and the postcondition `ensures Valid() && ...` cannot be proved. The intended behavior says initialisation takes a positive capacity, so the precondition is too weak: it should require c > 0.

Push only requires Valid(), which allows top == capacity - 1, i.e. a full stack. The body does top := top + 1 and then writes arr[top], so on a full stack it indexes arr[capacity], one past the end. The counterexample shows exactly this: capacity = 1, top = 0, then top = 1 = arr.Length. The intended behaviour says Push works on a stack that is not full, but that requirement is missing from the precondition. Without it the array write is unsafe and the ensures Valid() (top < capacity) cannot hold either.

pred_repair: forall i, j :: 0 <= start <= i <= j < end <= arr.Length ==> arr[i] <= arr[j]
pred_diagnosis: The errors are well-formedness failures inside the predicate 'sorted', not in sortArray's loops. 'sorted' has no precondition and its quantifier guard 'start <= i <= j < end' does not tie start and end to the array bounds. Dafny checks the predicate body for every possible argument. The counterexamples show this: with start = -39, arr[i] can be read at a negative index, and with end = 7681 > arr.Length = 2438, arr[j] can be read past the end. So both arr[i] and arr[j] at line 46 may be out of range. Adding only 'requires 0 <= start <= end <= arr.Length' would likely move the problem to the call sites. The outer invariant 'sorted(arr, 0, i)' and the inner 'sorted(arr, 0, i+1)' do not establish 0 <= i, because the loop only has the invariant i <= arr.Length. The safe fix is to put the bounds into the quantifier's range in the predicate body, which makes every call well-formed.

pred_repair: requires exists u, v :: 0 <= u < v < nums.Length && nums[u] + nums[v] == target
pred_diagnosis: The outer loop invariant on line 12 says a solution pair exists: exists u, v :: i <= u < v < nums.Length && nums[u] + nums[v] == target. At loop entry i == 0, so this needs a pair in the whole array that sums to target. The precondition only requires 2 <= nums.Length. It never states the intended assumption that such a pair exists, so the invariant cannot be established on entry (e.g. nums.Length = 7721, target = 0 with no pair summing to 0). The missing requires clause must state that a solution exists.

The precondition of RowColumnProduct says `column < (m2.Length1) + 1`, which allows column == m2.Length1. That is one past the last valid column index. The body calls RowColumnProductFrom, which requires `column < m2.Length1`, so the call's precondition cannot be proved. The counterexample shows exactly this case: column = 1236 = m2.Length1. The off-by-one `+ 1` weakened the requires clause so it no longer guarantees the callee's precondition.

The intended behavior is for a non-empty array, but the precondition was weakened to `a.Length > -1`, which allows `a.Length == 0`. The outer loop starts with `i := 1`, so for an empty array the first outer invariant `i <= a.Length` (line 26) becomes `1 <= 0`. That is false, so the invariant cannot be proved on entry. This matches the counterexample with `a.Length = 0` and `i = 1`. Requiring a non-empty array establishes the invariant at loop entry.

The method sets i := 1 before the outer loop, and the invariant i <= a.Length must hold on entry. The precondition `requires a.Length > -1` is vacuous because array lengths are never negative, so it allows an empty array. With a.Length == 0 and i == 1, the invariant i <= a.Length is false at loop entry, as the counterexample shows. The intended behavior is sorting a non-empty array, so the precondition is too weak.

SkipHead has no precondition, so it knows nothing about this node's structure. Without Valid(), Dafny cannot show that List is non-empty, so List[1..] in the ensures clause is reported as 'lower bound out of range'. It also cannot show that next.Valid() holds or that next.List == List[1..] and next.Repr <= Repr, so the postcondition fails on the return path even though the body (r := next) is correct. The method is missing its `requires Valid()` clause, which every other operation on a valid list has.

pred_repair: requires forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2;  // the elements of "a" in the range [0.. a.Length-2]
pred_diagnosis: The range precondition was weakened to allow -1 <= a[i], which contradicts its own comment that elements lie in [0..a.Length-2). Inside the second loop the body does `var k := d[a[i]]`. When a[i] == -1 this indexes d at -1, which is out of range. The counterexample has a[3089] = -1. Nothing else in the loop can rule this out, so the loop body cannot safely execute an iteration. The precondition must restrict elements to the valid index range of d, i.e. 0 <= a[i] < a.Length - 2 == d.Length.

pred_repair: requires exists p,q :: p != q && IsDuplicate(a, p) && IsDuplicate(a, q);  // two distinct duplicates exist
pred_diagnosis: The precondition stating that the array contains two distinct duplicated values was dropped. The second loop is `while (true)` and relies on the invariant `0 <= i < a.Length`. That invariant is maintained across `i := i + 1` only because the method is guaranteed to return (on finding the second duplicate) before i reaches a.Length. Without the assumption that two distinct duplicates exist, Dafny cannot rule out reaching the last element without finding a second duplicate, so `i + 1 < a.Length` cannot be proved. The counterexample shows an array with only one duplicated value (5596).

FIND's precondition only says 0 <= f < N. It does not relate N to the array length. The original Dafny test has `requires A.Length == N`. Without it, A[p], A[q] and A[f] can go out of bounds. This happens in the ensures clause (line 50), in the outer loop invariants (lines 55-56) and at `A[f]` (line 58). The counterexamples confirm it: A.Length = 0 with N = 1, and A.Length = 536 with N = 540. The ensures and invariants are well-formed only if N equals A.Length, so the missing precondition is the root cause.

The precondition of Lemma_Split was weakened to 'u <= |a| + 1', which lets t and u exceed |a|. Its ensures clause calls Count(a, s, t, x) and Count(a, s, u, x), and Count requires its upper bound to be at most |a|. So the postcondition is not well-formed: the specification does not guarantee Count's precondition, as the counterexamples with t or u equal to |a| + 1 show.

Client has no precondition, yet at line 75 it constructs the iterator with `new M(l, c)`, and M requires `l.Valid()`. Inside Client nothing tells Dafny that `l` is a well-formed List, so every conjunct of Valid() (this in Repr, a in Repr, n <= a.Length, Contents == a[..n]) is unprovable at the call. The counterexample shows this: it picks an arbitrary list with n > a.Length. Because the iterator cannot be constructed legally, the loop's starting state, including the invariants about iter, is never properly established. Main only calls Client on a list it knows is valid, so the intended contract of Client is that it receives a valid list.

The lemma crash_safe_single_tx weakens its precondition to 'countdown >= -1'. It then immediately calls init_ghost_state(init_log, init_mem, countdown), which requires 'countdown >= 0'. With countdown = -1, as in the counterexample, the callee's precondition fails, so the lemma's precondition does not establish what is needed at the start of the proof. The intended model uses a non-negative crash countdown, so the precondition should be 'countdown >= 0'. This error is separate from the timeout reported for UndoLog.recover.

The lemma bits_trim_front has the precondition `requires n > -1`. For a nat this is always true, so n == 0 is allowed. Then bits(0) == [] and the slice bits(n)[1..] is out of range, which makes the ensures clause ill-formed ('lower bound out of range'). For the same reason the postcondition cannot be proved when n == 0, matching the counterexample n = 0. The precondition is too weak: it should require n to be positive so that bits(n) has at least one element. In that case bits(n)[1..] == bits(n/2), and from_bits(bits(n/2)) == n/2 follows by the same induction that already proves bits_from_bits.

Gcd is meant to operate on positive numbers, but the precondition only constrains x1 (1 <= x1) and says nothing about x2. As a result the outer loop invariant 1 <= y1 && 1 <= y2 cannot be established on entry. The counterexample x1 = 1, x2 = 0 gives y2 = 0, which violates the invariant. The missing requirement on x2 must be restored in the precondition.

Lemma1 has no precondition on k. Its other callers pass a nonnegative k, but nothing inside Lemma1 itself rules out a negative k. As a result, the ensures clause SumEmUp(0, k) is not well-formed: SumEmUp requires 0 <= n <= m, which fails when k = -1. The loop invariant i <= k also cannot hold on entry, since i = 0 and k may be negative (the counterexample uses k = -2). The missing precondition 0 <= k is what both checks need.

The invariant `d <= r` (line 37) is false on loop entry whenever n < d. Initially r := n, and the precondition only requires n >= 0 and d > 0. For example, n = 0 and d = 1 give r = 0 < d. The invariant also contradicts the loop's purpose: on exit `!(r >= d)` must give r < d, which cannot coexist with `d <= r`. What actually holds on entry and is preserved, since r is decreased by d only when r >= d, is that r stays non-negative. Together with the exit condition r < d, that gives the required 0 <= r < d.

The recursive function gcd only requires m > 0, so n may be 0. The counterexample is m = 1, n = 0. Then m > n, and the call gcd(m - n, n) becomes gcd(1, 0) with exactly the same arguments, so it recurses forever. With n allowed to be 0, the default lexicographic measure (m, n) cannot be shown to decrease, and Dafny reports a termination failure at the recursive calls. The intended domain is two positive integers, and the method gcdI already requires both to be positive. The function's precondition is therefore too weak. If n > 0 is also required, then for m > n the call has m - n with 0 < m - n < m, and for m < n it has 0 < n - m < n with m unchanged. Both calls then decrease and both satisfy the precondition.

The predicate 'partitioned' reads a[k, 1] and a[k', 1] but has no precondition on a.Length1. The verifier checks the predicate body for well-formedness on its own, and nothing there guarantees that column index 1 is in range. The counterexample has a.Length1 = 1, where index 1 is out of bounds, which causes the 'index 1 out of range' error at line 80. The sibling predicate 'sorted' avoids this with 'requires a.Length1 == 2', and every caller (bubble_sort and its loop invariants) already ensures a.Length1 == 2, so adding the same precondition makes the predicate well-formed without breaking any call site.

The solver fails to close the gap between |l| = |old(l)| - 1 and the post-state this.capacity without an explicit old-qualified capacity bound in the same clause.

When a.Length == 0, we get 1 <= 0, which is false, so the invariant cannot be established on entry. The intended behavior specifies a non-empty array, so the precondition is too weak.

The method's precondition only states 0 <= f < N but does not relate N to the actual array length. All invariants (and the body) index into A with values up to N-1, so Dafny cannot prove the indices are in range. Every counterexample has N > A.Length (e.g., A.Length=0, N=1), causing 'index out of range' when checking well-formedness of the invariants at loop entry.

Lemma_Split's precondition allows u (and hence t) to reach |a|+1, but the postcondition invokes Count(a,s,t,x), Count(a,t,u,x), and Count(a,s,u,x), each of which requires its upper bound to satisfy <= |a|. With the current bound u <= |a|+1, Dafny cannot prove the Count calls are in range, so the postcondition is not well-formed. The counterexamples confirm this: t=1238, u=1238 with |a|=1237.

Inside Client, the call 'new M(l, c)' requires l.Valid() (the iterator M's precondition), but since Client made no assumption about l's validity, Dafny cannot prove this call precondition. The counterexample confirms this: it shows a state where n > a.Length, violating Valid(). The lemma crash_safe_single_tx declares 'requires countdown >= -1' but immediately calls init_ghost_state(init_log, init_mem, countdown), whose precondition is 'requires countdown >= 0'. When countdown = -1 (as in the counterexample), Dafny cannot prove the callee's precondition, so the function call fails verification. The lemma's precondition is too weak to establish what the body needs at the very first step.

The precondition `requires n > -1` is trivially true for all `nat` values (since nat is bounded below by 0). When n == 0, `bits(0)` returns the empty sequence `[]`, so the slice `bits(0)[1..]` in the postcondition is ill-formed (lower bound 1 exceeds length 0). This causes the 'lower bound out of range' well-formedness error. Even if well-formedness were satisfied, the empty body `{}` means the postcondition must follow directly from the precondition, but `from_bits(bits(0)[1..]) == 0/2` is not meaningful for the empty case. The precondition must exclude n == 0 so that `bits(n)` has at least one element.

The Gcd method's precondition only constrains x1 (requires 1 <= x1), leaving x2 unconstrained. At loop entry, y2 is initialized to x2, so the invariant 1 <= y1 && 1 <= y2 cannot be established when x2 < 1 (e.g., x2 = 0 as shown in the counterexample). The method's intended behavior is GCD on positive numbers, so x2 must also be positive.

Lemma1(k: int) has no precondition restricting k to be non-negative. Because k can be negative (e.g. k = -2), the loop invariant `i <= k` is false at loop entry when i = 0 (0 <= -2 fails). The same missing precondition also makes the ensures clause `SumEmUp(0, k)` ill-formed, since SumEmUp requires 0 <= n && n <= m, i.e. 0 <= k here. Adding `requires 0 <= k` to Lemma1 fixes both errors: the invariant `i <= k` holds on entry (0 <= k), and the SumEmUp(0,k) call in the ensures clause is well-formed.

The invariant `d <= r` cannot be proved on entry. At the point the loop is reached, q=0 and r=n, so the invariant requires d <= n. However, the precondition only states n >= 0 && d > 0, which does not imply d <= n (e.g., n=0, d=1). Even though the loop guard r >= d would prevent execution of the body in that case, Dafny still requires every invariant to hold at the loop entry point regardless of whether the guard is true.

The gcd function only requires m > 0 but not n > 0. Under the default lexicographic decreases (m, n), the recursive call gcd(m - n, n) in the branch m > n does not strictly decrease when n = 0 (it becomes gcd(m, 0), the same arguments). The counterexample m = 1, n = 0 confirms this: the function never reaches the base case and the measure is stuck. Adding n > 0 to the precondition ensures m - n > 0 in the m > n branch and n - m > 0 in the m < n branch, so both recursive calls strictly decrease lexicographically.

The predicate `partitioned` is missing a `requires a.Length1 == 2` clause. When Dafny checks the well-formedness of the loop invariant `partitioned(a, i)` at the initial state of the inner loop, it must prove that the index `1` in `a[k, 1]` and `a[k', 1]` is valid (i.e., `1 < a.Length1`).
